{{< include macros.qmd >}}

# Systems {#sec-systems}

::: {.callout-tip}

## Aims of the chapter

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

* Explain what a system of equations is and how it relates to higher order equations for both difference and differential equations.
* Solve $2 \times 2$ first order linear systems of difference equations with constant coefficients.
* Describe the general form of a solution of a inhomogeneous first order linear system of difference equations.
* Solve $2 \times 2$ first order linear systems of differential equations with constant coefficients.
* Analyse the stability and produce a phase portrait for a $2 \times 2$ first order autonomous systems of differential equations, both linear and nonlinear.

:::

So far, we have studied differential and difference equations for a single dependent variable. But in the same way as you can have systems of algebraic equations,^[You might know them as coupled equations.] you can also have systems of differential or difference equations. In fact, we already came across a system of differential equation in @exm-covid, where we saw the SEIR model for the spread of an infectious disease. In this chapter we will study systems of first order equations, that is systems composed of several first order equations. We will focus mostly on $2 \times 2$ systems, but most of the ideas and concepts generalise to all $n \times n$ systems, $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

::: {.callout-note}
Unless stated otherwise for the whole of this chapter we assume that any functions involved in the systems are sufficiently "nice", such that there is a unique solution of the system of equations we are considering.
:::

## Systems of difference equations

We start by considering systems of difference equations.

::: {#def-system-difference-equations-m-by-m}

In their most general form, a first order system of difference equations can be written as
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1,k+1} &= f_1 \left( x_{1,k},x_{2,k},\ldots,x_{n,k}, k \right), \\
x_{2,k+1} &= f_2 \left( x_{1,k},x_{2,k},\ldots,x_{n,k}, k \right), \\
&\vdots \\
x_{n,k+1} &= f_n \left( x_{1,k},x_{2,k},\ldots,x_{n,k}, k \right),
\end{aligned}
$$
for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and with some initial conditions $x_{1,0},x_{2,0},\ldots,x_{n,0}$. Here $x_{i,k}$ is the $i$th dependent variable at step $k$, $f_i: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ are given functions, and $n$ is the number of equations and variables in the system. The system is called an $n \times n$ system of first order difference equations.^[To be precise, the most general form would be something of the form $f(...) = 0$, as we did with differential equations, but the notation would get even messier so we will stick to the above form.]
:::

It is often convenient to write the system in vector form.^[In this module we will consider vectors to be column vectors, hence why we have all the transpose operations.] This is simply a relabelling of the variables and functions. Let $\boldsymbol{x}_k = (x_{1,k},x_{2,k},\ldots,x_{n,k})^T$ and $\boldsymbol{f} = (f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_n)^T$. Then we can write the system as
$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = \boldsymbol{f} \left( \boldsymbol{x}_k, k \right),
$$
where $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is known and $\boldsymbol{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector-valued function.

We do not give a formal definition, but note that the same classification of difference equations that we introduced in @def-difference-equation-properties naturally generalises to systems. In particular, the order of the system is still the difference between the highest and lowest index of the dependent variables and the system is linear if $\boldsymbol{f}$ is linear.

::: {.callout-important}
For simplicity, in this module we will focus on $2\times2$ systems of first order difference equations of the form, and to simplify the notation we will usually write them in the form

$$
\begin{split}
x_{k+1} = f_1 \left( x_k,y_k,k \right), \\
y_{k+1} = f_2 \left( x_k,y_k,k \right),
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-elem-diff}

with $k \in \mathbb{N}$, some given functions $f_i: \mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$, $i=1,2$ and initial conditions $x_0$ and $y_0$. This is equivalent to the notation in @def-system-difference-equations-m-by-m but using $x_k$ and $y_k$ instead of $x_{1,k}$ and $x_{2,k}$ to simplify the notation.
:::

### Relation to higher order equations

::: {.callout-important}
::: {#lem-second-order-difference-to-system}
Any (scalar) second order difference equation can be written as a $2\times2$ system of first order equations.
:::

:::

::: {.proof}
Recalling the definition of a general scalar difference equation, let

$$
x_{k+2}=f(x_{k+1},x_k,k)
$$

be any second order equation.

Now let $y_k=x_{k+1}$. Then $y_{k+1}=x_{k+2}$ and we can reformulate the equation in the form

$$\begin{aligned}
y_{k+1}&=f(y_k,x_k,k)\,,\\
x_{k+1}&=y_k\,.
\end{aligned}$$

This is a $2\times2$ system.
:::

::: {#rem-mxm-generalisation}
The above concepts for $2\times2$ systems can be generalised to $n\times n$ systems for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ in a straightforward way.
:::

::: {#exm-second-order-difference-to-system}
Consider the second order difference equation

$$
x_{k+2}+e^kx_{k+1}+10x_k=\log(k)\,.
$$

Writing $y_k=x_{k+1}$ we obtain the system

$$\begin{aligned}
y_{k+1}+e^ky_k+10x_k&=\log(k)\,, \\
x_{k+1}&=y_k\,.
\end{aligned}$$

:::

As we can rewrite the second order equations as a system, this raises the question whether we can do so the other way round as well. In general, this is not possible, however sometimes we can do so.

::: {#exm-system-to-second-order-difference}
Consider the system

$$\begin{aligned}
x_{k+1}=\sin(k)x_k+y_k\,,\\
y_{k+1}=x_k\,.
\end{aligned}$$

Substituting $x_k=y_{k+1}$ and $x_{k+1}=y_{k+2}$ into the first equations, we get

$$
y_{k+2}=\sin(k)y_{k+1}+y_k.
$$

:::

### Linear systems with constant coefficients

Let us now briefly talk about how one solves $2 \times 2$ linear systems of difference equations with constant coefficients. This is systems of the form
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{k+1} &= a_{1,1} x_k + a_{1,2} y_k,\\
y_{k+1} &= a_{2,1} x_k + a_{2,2} y_k,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-linear-system-difference-constant-coefficients}
for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and some initial conditions. 

Note that, defining the matrix
$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} \\ a_{2,1} & a_{2,2} \end{pmatrix},
$$
the system can be written, in vector form, as
$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = A \boldsymbol{x}_k.
$$

A simple way to solve the system would be to convert it into a second order difference equation (as it is linear, we will always be able to) and solve it as we did in @sec-difference-equations-second-order. However, we can also solve the system directly using the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix $A$. This is a more general approach that can be used for any $n \times n$ linear system of difference equations with constant coefficients.

However, let us study it as a system. Similarly to what we did in @sec-linear-first-order-difference-equations-homogeneous, we can calculate the first few values of $\boldsymbol{x}_k$ to deduce a pattern:
$$\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}_1 &= A \boldsymbol{x}_0,  \\
\boldsymbol{x}_2 &= A \boldsymbol{x}_1 = A^2 \boldsymbol{x}_0,  \\
\boldsymbol{x}_3 &= A \boldsymbol{x}_2 = A^3 \boldsymbol{x}_0,  \\
\vdots  \\
\boldsymbol{x}_k &= A^k \boldsymbol{x}_0.
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-diffeqnfosoln}
Here, $A^k$ is the $k$th power of the matrix $A$, i.e. $A^k = A \cdot A \dots \cdot A$ ($k$ times). Therefore, the solution to the system can be expressed as $\boldsymbol{x}_k = A^k \boldsymbol{x}_0$. Of course, one needs to compute $A^k$ to get the solution. We will not do this in this module, but if you take a linear algebra module, you will learn how to do that using the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A$.

## Systems of differential equations

Let us now consider first order systems of differential equations. In vector notation, the most general form of an $m \times m$ first order system of differential equations is
$$
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}} \left( t,\boldsymbol{x}(t), \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) \right) = \boldsymbol{0}, \quad \text{with} \quad \boldsymbol{x}(t_0) = \boldsymbol{x}_0,
$$ {#eq-system-differential-general}
where $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{F}}: (\alpha,\beta) \times (\mathbb{R}^m)^2 \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a given function, $\boldsymbol{x}(t) = (x_1(t),x_2(t),\ldots,x_m(t))^T$ is the vector of dependent variables, and $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a given initial condition. 

::: {.callout-important}
In this module we will constrain ourselves to studying $2 \times 2$ systems of first order equations, and we will assume we can always write them in the form
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x(t) &= f_1 \left( x(t),y(t),t \right), & \text{with} \quad x(t_0) &= x_0,\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} y(t) &= f_2 \left( x(t),y(t),t \right), & \text{with} \quad y(t_0) &= y_0,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-2x2-system-differential}
for $t \in (\alpha,\beta)$ and with some given functions $f_i: \mathbb{R}^2 \times (\alpha,\beta) \to \mathbb{R}$, where $i=1,2$. 

:::

::: {#rem-systems-differential-2x2}
A couple of remarks. First, as it happened with systems of difference equations, the definitions of order, linearity, etc. that we introduced for scalar differential equations in @def-deq-basics generalise to systems of differential equations. Second, we will interchangeably use the notation $x(t)$, $y(t)$ and $x_1(t)$, $x_2(t)$ for the dependent variables, depending on which is more convenient in the context.
:::

Note that we assumed that  $t$ belongs to the open interval $(\alpha,\beta)$. If $t_{0} = \alpha$ or $t_{0} = \beta$ then we implicitly assume that we can extend the solution to these boundary points.

### Relation to higher order equations

::: {.callout-important}
::: {#lem-second-order-ode-to-system}
Any (scalar) second order differential equation can be written as a $2 \times 2$ system of first order equations.
:::
:::

Recalling the definition @eq-deq-general of a general scalar differential equation, let

$$
\mathcal{F}(x,y(x),y'(x),y''(x)) = 0
$$

be any second order equation. Let now $\eta(x) = y'(x)$. Then $\eta'(x) = y''(x)$ and we can reformulate the equation in the form

$$\begin{aligned}
y'(x) - \eta(x) &= 0, \\
\mathcal{F}(x,y(x),\eta(x),\eta'(x)) &= 0.
\end{aligned}$$

This is a $2 \times 2$ system of the most general form @eq-system-differential-general. These concepts for $2 \times 2$ systems can be generalised to $n \times n$ systems for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ in a straightforward way, including rewriting higher order equations of $n$th order as a system.

::: {#exm-second-order-ode-to-system}
Consider the second order equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t^2} x + \cos(t) \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x - x^2 = 0.
$$

Writing $x_1(t) = x(t)$ and $x_2(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1(t)$ we obtain the system

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1 - x_2 = 0, \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2 + \cos(t) x_2 - x_1^2 = 0.
$$

:::

As we can rewrite the second order equation as a system this raises the question whether we can do so the other way round as well. In general, this is not possible, however sometimes we can do so.

::: {#exm-system-to-second-order-ode}
Consider the system

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1 &= x_1 + x_2, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2 &= 4x_1 - 2x_2 + 4 e^{-2t}.
\end{aligned}$$

Rearranging the first equation we see that

$$
x_2 = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1 - x_1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2 = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t^2} x_1 - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1.
$$

Therefore, using the second equation,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t^2} x_1 - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1 = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2 = 4x_1 - 2x_2 + 4 e^{-2t} = 4x_1 - 2\Big{(} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1 - x_1 \Big{)} + 4 e^{-2t}.
$$

Rearranging yields the second order equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t^2} x_1 + \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1 - 6 x_1 = 4 e^{-2t}.
$$

:::

## Linear systems

We will first focus on linear systems of differential equations, particularly with constant coefficients. Before we analyse the latter in more detail in @sec-linear-systems-constant-coefficients, we first establish some more general results for linear systems where the coefficients can depend on the independent variable. These are of the form

::: {.callout-important}
$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1(t) = a_{1,1}(t) x_1(t) + a_{1,2}(t) x_2(t) + s_{1}(t),  \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2(t) = a_{2,1}(t) x_1(t) + a_{2,2}(t) x_2(t) + s_{2}(t),
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-lin}

where the $a_{i,j} : [\alpha,\beta] \to \mathbb{R}$ and the $s_i: [\alpha,\beta] \to \mathbb{R}$ are given functions, $i,j \in \{ 1,2 \}$. 

We can formulate this system in matrix-vector form as follows:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) = A(t) \boldsymbol{x}(t) + \boldsymbol{s}(t),
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix}
with
$$\qquad A(t) = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1}(t) & a_{1,2}(t) \\ a_{2,1}(t) & a_{2,2}(t) \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, \quad \boldsymbol{x}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x_1(t) \\ x_2(t) \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{s}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} s_1(t) \\ s_2(t) \end{pmatrix}.
$$ 
This notation, in addition to being more compact, allows us to use the tools of linear algebra to study the system later on.

:::

### Homogeneous system, complementary function

::: {.callout-important}
We first study the homogeneous case $\boldsymbol{s}(t) = 0$ for all $t \in [\alpha,\beta]$ in @eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix, i.e.
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) = A(t) \boldsymbol{x}(t),
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-lin-hom}
with some suitable initial condition.

Suppose that $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t)$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t)$ are two solutions. Thanks to the linearity of the differential equation any *linear combination*

$$
l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t), \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \, t \in (\alpha,\beta),
$$ {#eq-lincomb}

then is a solution, too.

::: {#def-linearly-independent-vector-functions}
## Linearly independent functions

Two functions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)} : [\alpha,\beta] \to \mathbb{R}^2$ are *linearly independent*^[The concept of linear independence naturally extends from the scalar case to the vector case.] if the only solution of

$$
c_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + c_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = 0 \quad \text{for any } c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}
$$ {#eq-linindep}

at all times $t \in [\alpha,\beta]$ is $c_1=c_2=0$.

:::
:::

Observe that in the this case where we have two functions only, linear dependence effectively means that the two functions are multiples of each other, because if $c_1,c_2 \neq 0$ exist then we can write $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) = -\frac{c_2}{c_1} \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t)$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)} = - \frac{c_1}{c_2} \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}.$ (We here omit a tedious discussion of trivial cases when any of the functions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(i)}$ or any of the coefficients $c_i$ is zero.)

::: {#exm-linear-independence-vector-functions}
Consider $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) = (t,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = (t^2,t)$ for $t \in [0,2]$ and let $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ be such that

$$
c_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + c_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \begin{pmatrix} c_1 t + c_2 t^2 \\ c_1 + c_2 t \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$

at all times $t \in [0,2]$. Choosing $t=0$ we see from the second equation that necessarily $c_1 = 0$. If we then choose $t=2$ then the second equation yields that $2 c_2 = 0$, so necessarily $c_2 = 0$ as well.

Note that we are free to choose the time. In fact, if we only consider a specific time we might get a wrong answer. Say, if we only consider $t=1$ then both equations read $c_1 + c_2 = 0$, and there are many solutions to this equation, for instance, $c_1 = 42$ and $c_2 = -42$.

:::

::: {.callout-important}
::: {#thm-2x2sys-solset}
Assume that $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)} : (\alpha,\beta) \to \mathbb{R}^2$ are two linearly independent solutions of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom. Then all solutions are of the form

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t), \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \, t \in [\alpha,\beta].
$$

Moreover, if an initial condition of the form

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t_{0}) = \boldsymbol{x_{0}} \in \mathbb{R}^2 \quad \text{for some } t_{0} \in [\alpha,\beta]
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-ic}

is imposed then $l_1,l_2$ are given as the unique solution of

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{0} = l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t_{0}) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t_{0}).
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-iclinsys}

:::

::: {.proof}
We omit the details of the proof, but it follows easily from substituting the linear combination @eq-lincomb into the system @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom and using the linear independence of $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ to show that any solution must be of this form. The uniqueness of $l_1,l_2$ follows from the linear independence as well.
:::

::: {#def-complementary-function-system}
## Complementary function

Given any two linearly independent solutions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}$, $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ of the $2 \times 2$ linear system of homogeneous differential equation @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom, the set of functions

$$
l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)} + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)} : (\alpha,\beta) \to \mathbb{R}^2, \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R},
$$

is called *general solution* or *complementary function*.

:::
:::

In summary, @thm-2x2sys-solset implies that this general solution is the set of *all* solutions to the differential equation, and if an initial condition of the form @eq-2x2sys-ic is imposed then the system @eq-2x2sys-iclinsys has to be solved to identify the then unique coefficients $l_1,l_2$.

### Inhomogeneous system, particular integral

Let us now consider the inhomogeneous case, i.e. @eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix where $\boldsymbol{s}(t) \neq \boldsymbol{0}$ for at least some $t \in (\alpha,\beta)$. It turns out that knowing only one solution to the differential equation is sufficient to find all solutions and the one for a specific initial condition.

::: {.callout-important}
::: {#thm-2x2sys-solsetinhom}
## Particular integral

Assume that $\boldsymbol{x}_{p}: (\alpha,\beta) \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is a solution to the inhomogeneous system @eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix, called the *particular integral*, and that $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)} : (\alpha,\beta) \to \mathbb{R}^2$ are two linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous system @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom. Then all solutions to the inhomogeneous system
@eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix are of the form

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) + l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t), \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \, t \in [\alpha,\beta].
$$

Moreover, if we impose an initial condition of the form in @eq-2x2sys-ic, then $l_1,l_2$ are given as the unique solution of

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{0} - \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t_{0}) = l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t_{0}) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t_{0}).
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-iclinsysinhom}

:::
:::

::: {.proof}

Assume that $\boldsymbol{x}$ is a solution of the inhomogeneous system @eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix. Define now the function $\boldsymbol{x}_{h}(t) = \boldsymbol{x}(t) - \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t)$, $t \in (\alpha,\beta)$. Observe that it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}_{h}(t) &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \left( \boldsymbol{x}(t) - \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) \right) \\
&= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) - \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) \\
&= A(t) \boldsymbol{x}(t) + s(t) - A(t) \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) - s(t) \\
&= A(t) \left( \boldsymbol{x}(t) - \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) \right) \\
&= A(t) \boldsymbol{x}_{h}(t),
\end{aligned}$$

so $\boldsymbol{x}_{h}$ is a solution to the homogeneous system @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom. From @thm-2x2sys-solset we know that its solutions are of the form

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_{h}(t) = l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t), \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \, t \in [\alpha,\beta].
$$

Altogether, $\boldsymbol{x}(t) = \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) + \boldsymbol{x}_{h}(t) = \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t) + l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t)$ is of the form as claimed.

We may proceed as in the proof of @thm-2x2sys-solset to show that @eq-2x2sys-iclinsysinhom has a unique solution $l_1,l_2$. Then

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t_{0}) = \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t_{0}) + l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t_{0}) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t_{0}) = \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t_{0}) + \boldsymbol{x}_{0} - \boldsymbol{x}_{p}(t_{0}) = \boldsymbol{x}_{0},
$$

so $\boldsymbol{x}$ also satisfies the correct initial condition. As we assume that the system is well-posed, the solution to the initial value problem is unique, so there is no solution other than $\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_{p} + l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)} + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$.

:::

Such a solution $\boldsymbol{x}_{p}$ of the inhomogeneous system @eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix is known in the literature as a *particular integral*. We see in @thm-2x2sys-solsetinhom how it can be used together with solutions to the corresponding homogeneous system to synthesize the solution to the initial value problem as a linear combination. This idea is called *superposition principle* and generally works for linear models, not only for differential equations. In practice, finding a particular integral can be quite challenging, though.

## Homogeneous linear systems with constant coefficients {#sec-linear-systems-constant-coefficients}

We learned in the previous section that two linearly independent solutions to the linear system (plus one particular integral in the inhomogeneous case) are sufficient to solve any initial value problem. In the case of constant coefficients it is actually possible to find such two linearly independent solutions.

::: {.callout-important}
Let us look into linear systems of the form

$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1(t) = a_{1,1} x_1(t) + a_{1,2} x_2(t), \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2(t) = a_{2,1} x_1(t) + a_{2,2} x_2(t),
\end{split}
\quad t \in \mathbb{R},
$$

where the $a_{i,j} \in \mathbb{R}$ now are independent of $t$. These can be formulated in the matrix-vector form
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) = A \boldsymbol{x}(t), \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} \\ a_{2,1} & a_{2,2} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}, \quad \boldsymbol{x}(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x_1(t) \\ x_2(t) \end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc}
:::

We found that exponential functions have been working well with the linear equations that we saw so far, so let us try to find a solution in the form
$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t} \boldsymbol{v},
$$
where $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ are to be determined from the system.

Substituting this approach in the system yields

$$
\lambda e^{\lambda t} \boldsymbol{v} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) = A \boldsymbol{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t} A \boldsymbol{v}.
$$

Using that $e^{\lambda t} \neq 0$ we obtain that

$$
\lambda \boldsymbol{v} = A \boldsymbol{v}.
$$ {#eq-eigenvec}

So $\boldsymbol{x}(t) = e^{\lambda t} \boldsymbol{v}$ is a solution if $\lambda$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$ solve @eq-eigenvec. It turns out that there are at most two distinct pairs of $\lambda$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$ that solve this equation. For a given matrix $A$, values of $\lambda$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$ that satisfy @eq-eigenvec are called the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix. We will discuss them in more detail in @sec-eigenvalues-eigenvectors. 

### Eigenvalues and eigenvectors {#sec-eigenvalues-eigenvectors}

In general, the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most two distinct eigenvalues (similarly, an $n\times n$ matrix would have at most $n$ distinct eigenvalues) and each eigenvalue is paired with a corresponding eigenvector solving @eq-eigenvec. Assuming this is the case we denote them by $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors by $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$. These eigenvectors are always linearly independent.^[This will be proved in [MA149 Linear Algebra](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/currentstudents/modules/ma149/)]

::: {.callout-important}

::: {#def-eigenvalues}
The eigenvalues of a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$ are the roots to its *characteristic polynomial*, $\det(\lambda I-A)=0$.
:::

This gives the polynomial

$$
\lambda^2-(a_{1,1}+a_{2,2})\lambda+a_{1,1}a_{2,2}-a_{2,1}a_{1,2}\,,
$$

with roots

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{a_{1,1} + a_{2,2}}{2} \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(a_{1,1} - a_{2,2})^2 + 4 a_{2,1} a_{1,2}}.
$$ {#eq-eigenvalues-2x2}

::: {#rem-eigenvalues-complex}
## Complex eigenvalues

From @eq-eigenvalues-2x2 we see that the eigenvalues could be complex. In this case, the corresponding eigenvectors are also complex, so from now on we will allow $\boldsymbol{v}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{C}^2$ and $\lambda_i \in \mathbb{C}$, $i=1,2$.

:::

::: {#def-eigenvectors}
The corresponding eigenvectors $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$ to eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are the solutions $\boldsymbol{v}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{C}^2$, $\boldsymbol{v}^{(i)} \neq (0,0)$, of

$$
(\lambda_{i} I - A) \boldsymbol{v}^{(i)} = 0, \quad i=1,2.
$$

There are two equations, and if $\boldsymbol{v}^{(i)}$ is an eigenvector then also every multiple $c \boldsymbol{v}^{(i)}$, $c \in \mathbb{C}$, is an eigenvector again. In practice, we just choose an arbitrary instance of $c \boldsymbol{v}^{(i)}$ to represent the eigenvector, for instance, by setting one of the components to $1$ and solving for the other component.

:::

:::

::: {#exm-eigenvalues-eigenvectors-2x2}
Consider the matrix

$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

In this case $a_{1,1} = 1$, $a_{1,2} = 2$, $a_{2,1} = 1$ and $a_{2,2} = 0$ so that

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{1-4(-2)} = \frac{1}{2} \pm \frac{3}{2},
$$

therefore $\lambda_1 = 2$ and $\lambda_2 = -1$. An eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = (v_1^{(1)},v_2^{(1)})$ corresponding to $\lambda_1$ satisfies

$$
0 = (\lambda_1 I - A) \boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 - 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v_1^{(1)} \\ v_2^{(1)} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} v_1^{(1)} - 2 v_2^{(1)} \\ -v_1^{(1)} + 2 v_2^{(1)} \end{pmatrix}.
$$

We see that a solution is given by $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = (2,1)$. Let us briefly check that this is an eigenvalue for $\lambda_1$:

$$
A \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = 2 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \lambda_1 \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}.
$$

Regarding $\lambda_2$, a corresponding eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = (v_1^{(2)},v_2^{(2)})$ satisfies

$$
0 = (\lambda_2 I - A) \boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 - 1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1 - 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v_1^{(2)} \\ v_2^{(2)} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 v_1^{(2)} - 2 v_2^{(2)} \\ -v_1^{(2)} - v_2^{(2)} \end{pmatrix}.
$$

A solution to these equations is $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = (1,-1)$, and it can be checked similarly.

:::

### Solving homogeneous linear systems with constant coefficients

We now have that for eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ with corresponding eigenvectors $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$, the functions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) = e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$ then are solutions to the homogenenous system of linear equations with constant coefficients, @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc. Moreover, these solutions are linearly independent.^[Just evaluate them at $t=0$ to obtain the $\boldsymbol{v}^{(i)}$, which are linearly independent.] The previous results on linear systems apply, in particular @thm-2x2sys-solset.^[Actually, we have studied the real-valued case only, but the steps of the proof still are valid if the functions $\boldsymbol{x}^{(i)} : (\alpha,\beta) \to \mathbb{C}^2$ are complex-valued and if the $l_i$ are complex.]

::: {.callout-important}
Hence, all solutions of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc are of the form of the complementary function,

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = l_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + l_2 e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}, \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{C},
$$

and the unique solution to the initial value problem consisting of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc and @eq-2x2sys-ic is obtained by substituting $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ and solving for $l_1,l_2$.
:::

Like we did with second order linear equations, we will now consider three separate cases for the eigenvalues of $A$ and discuss the corresponding solutions to the system of differential equations.^[At this point you probably have noticed the similiarities between $2\times2$ linear systems and second order linear equations. You can dig deeper in this similarity by converting a second order linear equation into a $2\times2$ linear system and vice versa, as we did in @exm-system-to-second-order-ode, and solving both.]

### Real eigenvalues

::: {.callout-important}
If $(a_{1,1} - a_{2,2})^2 + 4 a_{2,1} a_{1,2} > 0$ then the two eigenvalues are real and distinct and the corresponding eigenvectors $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}, \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ are linearly independent. The functions

$$
\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) = e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}, \quad \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}
$$

are then are linearly independent solutions, with general solution

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = l_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + l_2 e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}\,.
$$

Then the initial conditions $\boldsymbol{x}(t_0)=\boldsymbol{x}_0$ can be used to determine $l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {#exm-SysLinExA}
Consider @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc with an initial condition of the form @eq-2x2sys-ic where $t_{0} = 0$ and

$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 6 \\ -2 & -5 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of $A$ satisfy $\lambda^2 + 3 \lambda + 2 = 0$ and are

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = -\frac{3}{2} \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{3^2 - 4 \cdot 2} \quad \implies \quad \lambda_1 = -1, \quad \lambda_2 = -2.
$$

An eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}$ has to satisfy

$$
0 = (\lambda_1 I - A) \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 & -6 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}.
$$

A possible choice is $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = (-2,1)$. Proceeding similarly for $\lambda_2$ we find that a corresponding eigenvector is given by $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = (-3,2)$.

A general solution to the differential equations is thus given by

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = l_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + l_2 e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = l_1 e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 e^{-2t} \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad l_1, l_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

The initial condition is satisfied if

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{x}(0) = l_1 \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + l_2 \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = l_1 \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The solution to this $2 \times 2$ systems is $l_1 = -2$, $l_2 = 1$, so the unique solution of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc, @eq-2x2sys-ic with the above data is

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t) = -2 e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + e^{-2t} \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

@fig-example-linear-system-real-evs shows the solution in the $x_1$-$x_2$ plane. To facilitate the understanding of the solution, the arrows indicate the direction of the solution at each point $\boldsymbol{x}$, which is given by $A \boldsymbol{x}$.^[I have normalised the arrows to have the same length, so it is easier to read.]

As $\lambda_2<\lambda_1<0$ the solution converges to $(0,0)$ as $t \to \infty$ and, you can imagine, that if either of the eigenvalues were positive then the solution would diverge to infinity. We will discuss this in more detail in @sec-phase-portraits. 
:::

::: {layout="[[-25,50,-25]]"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-example-linear-system-real-evs
#| fig-cap: "Plot of the solution of @exm-SysLinExA."
#| echo: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from utils import apply_style, plot_phase_portrait

apply_style()

# ── System matrix ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

     [ -2, -5]]

# ── Start points for trajectories ────────────────────────────────────────────

# ── Layout: info panel (top, fixed height) + phase portrait (below) ──────────

    backward = False,
    ax_info  = ax_info,   # pass the info panel here
```

:::

### Complex eigenvalues

::: {.callout-important}
If $(a_{1,1} - a_{2,2})^2 + 4 a_{2,1} a_{1,2} < 0$ then the two eigenvalues are complex and satisfy

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{a_{1,1} + a_{2,2}}{2} \pm \frac{i}{2} \sqrt{- 4 a_{2,1} a_{1,2} - (a_{1,1} - a_{2,2})^2} \,,
$$

where $\lambda_{2} = \overline{\lambda_1}$ (complex conjugate).
:::

Moreover $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} \in \mathbb{C}^2$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1$ if and only if its conjugate $\overline{\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}}$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda_1}$. We do not prove it here, but combining both results we obtain
$$
\overline{e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}} = e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}.
$$

Recall that any linear combinations

$$
l_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + l_2 e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}, \quad l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{C},
$$

are solutions to the system of differential equations. But note that the real and imaginary parts of each independent solution can be written as a linear combination of the two independent solutions:
$$\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) &= \mathrm{Re} \left[ e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} \right] = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + \overline{e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}} \right) = \frac{1}{2} e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} + \frac{1}{2} e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = \mathrm{Re} \left[ e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} \right], \\
\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) &= \mathrm{Im} \left[ e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} \right] = \frac{1}{2i} \left( e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} - \overline{e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}} \right) = \frac{1}{2i} e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} - \frac{1}{2i} e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = - \mathrm{Im} \left[ e^{\lambda_2 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} \right]\,,
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathrm{Re}$ represents the real component, $p$, of a complex number $p+iq$ and $\mathrm{Im}$ represents the imaginary component, $q$.

To identify and further work out real and imaginary parts let us write

$$
\lambda_1 = p + i \omega \text{ with } p,\omega \in \mathbb{R}, \quad \text{and } \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = \boldsymbol{r} + i \boldsymbol{b} \text{ with } \boldsymbol{r}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

Note that $\omega \neq 0$, and one can show that $\boldsymbol{r} \neq (0,0)$ and $\boldsymbol{b} \neq (0,0)$.
Then

$$
e^{\lambda_1 t} = e^{pt} (\cos(\omega t) + i \sin(\omega t)),
$$

and consequently

$$\begin{aligned}
e^{\lambda_1 t} \boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} &= e^{pt} \left( \cos(\omega t) + i \sin(\omega t) \right) (\boldsymbol{r} + i \boldsymbol{b}) \\
&= e^{pt} \left( \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} - \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right) + i e^{pt} \left( \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} + \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right).
\end{aligned}$$

::: {.callout-important}
Two linearly independent real-valued solutions therefore are

$$
\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) = e^{pt} \left( \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} - \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right), \quad \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t) = e^{pt} \left( \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} + \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right).
$$

We obtain a general (real-valued) solution of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}(t) &= l_1 \boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t) + l_2 \boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t)\\
&= l_1 e^{pt} \left( \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} - \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right) + l_2 e^{pt} \left( \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} + \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-lin-cmpl-sol-final}

for $l_1,l_2 \in \mathbb{R}$.

Any initial condition of the form @eq-2x2sys-ic with $t_{0} = 0$ (this is only for in the notation simplicity) then becomes

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{x}(0) = l_1\boldsymbol{r} + l_2 \boldsymbol{b}.
$$

:::

::: {#rem-complex-eigenvalues-spirals}
Note that $\cos$ and $\sin$ will give rise to oscillations, which in the two-dimensional case manifest as spiralling around. For $p=0$ this will become a circle, maintaining a fixed distance away from $(0,0)$.
:::

::: {#exm-SysLinExB}
Consider @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc with an initial condition of the form @eq-2x2sys-ic where $t_{0} = 0$ and

$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ -1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of $A$ satisfy $\lambda^2 + 2 \lambda + 2 = 0$ and are

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = - \frac{2}{2} \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2^2 - 4 \cdot 2} = -1 \pm i, \quad \text{so } p=-1, \, \omega = 1.
$$

An eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1$ can be worked out to be

$$
\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 + i \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{so } \boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}, \, \boldsymbol{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

A general solution to the differential equations is thus given by

$$\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}(t) &= l_1 e^{pt} \left( \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} - \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right) + l_2  e^{pt} \left( \sin(\omega t) \boldsymbol{r} + \cos(\omega t) \boldsymbol{b} \right) \\
&= l_1 e^{-t} \cos(t) \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} - l_1 e^{-t} \sin(t) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 e^{-t} \sin(t) \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 e^{-t} \cos(t) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \\
&= l_1 e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 5 \cos(t) \\ -2 \cos(t) - \sin(t) \end{pmatrix} + l_2 e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 5 \sin(t) \\ -2 \sin(t) + \cos(t) \end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$$

The initial condition is satisfied if

$$
\boldsymbol{x}_0 = l_1 \boldsymbol{r} + l_2 \boldsymbol{b} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = l_1 \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Hence $l_1 = 4$ and $l_2 = 8$, and the unique solution of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc, @eq-2x2sys-ic with the above data is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}(t) &= e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 20 \cos(t) \\ -8 \cos(t) - 4 \sin(t) \end{pmatrix} + e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 40 \sin(t) \\ -16 \sin(t) + 8 \cos(t) \end{pmatrix} \\
&= e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 20 \cos(t) + 40 \sin(t) \\ - 20 \sin(t) \end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The plot of the solution is shown in @fig-example-linear-system-complex-evs. Because $e^{-t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$, the solution converges to $(0,0)$ as $t \to \infty$. Notice the difference from @fig-example-linear-system-real-evs: now the solutions "spiral" into the origin rather than "hitting" it directly.

:::

::: {layout="[[-25,50,-25]]"}

```{python}
# ── Layout: info panel (top, fixed height) + phase portrait (below) ──────────

gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(2, 1, height_ratios=[1, 5], figure=fig)

ax_info = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])   # info panel — fixed height ratio
ax      = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])   # phase portrait

plot_phase_portrait(
    ax,
    A        = A,
    starts   = starts,
    xlim     = (-1.5, 1.5),
    ylim     = (-1.5, 1.5),
    t_max    = 4,
    n_grid   = 20,
    t_arrows = [1, 2],
    alpha    = 0.4,
    backward = False,
    ax_info  = ax_info,   # pass the info panel here
)

plt.show()
```

:::

### Repeated real eigenvalue

It can happen that the two eigenvalues of $A$ coincide. If $(a_{1,1} - a_{2,2})^2 + 4 a_{2,1} a_{1,2} = 0$, then we have $\lambda=\lambda_1=\lambda_2\in\mathbb{R}$. In this instance we also only get one eigenvector, $\boldsymbol{v}$, and we have that $\boldsymbol{x}^{(1)}(t)=e^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}$ is still a solution to our first order $2\times2$ system. So we require a second, linearly independent, solution.

For scalar second order differential equations with repeated real roots of the auxiliary equation we saw that we could take $x(t)=te^{\lambda t}$ as a solution, so we try the ansatz

$$
\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t)=te^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}+e^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}
$$

for some vector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$ that is linearly independent to our eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}$. We want to check that this is a solution and find a formula for $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$.

We start by differentiating $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ and setting equal to $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}^{(2)}=A\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}$ to get

$$
\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}^{(2)}(t)=e^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}+t\lambda e^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}+\lambda e^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}=te^{\lambda t}A\boldsymbol{v}+e^{\lambda t}A\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}\,.
$$

Now we divide through by $e^{\lambda t}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{v}+t\lambda \boldsymbol{v}+\lambda \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}=tA\boldsymbol{v}+e^{\lambda t}A\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}=t\lambda\boldsymbol{v}+e^{\lambda t}A\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}
$$

since $A\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}$, which cancels and rearranges to give

$$
\boldsymbol{v}=(A-\lambda I)\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}\,.
$$

::: {.callout-important}
So now we have that $\boldsymbol{x}^{(2)}(t)$ solves our linear $2\times2$ system if $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{v}=(A-\lambda I)\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$, and our full general solution is given by

$$
\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\big(l_1e^{\lambda t} + l_2te^{\lambda t}\big)\boldsymbol{v}+l_2e^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}\,.
$$

:::

::: {#exm-SysLinExC}
Now consider @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc with an initial condition of the form @eq-2x2sys-ic where $t_{0} = 0$ and

$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues satisfy $\lambda^2 + 2 \lambda + 1 = 0$, therefore
$$
\lambda = -1,
$$
and we have a repeated eigenvalue. The corresponding eigenvector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(1)}$ (also repeated) is

$$
\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

We now need to find a vector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$ such that

$$
\boldsymbol{v} = (A - \lambda I)\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}, \quad \implies \quad \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}.
$$
A solution to this equation is $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)} = (0,1)$.

Then, a general solution to the differential equations is thus given by

$$\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}(t) &= \left( l_1 e^{-t} + l_2 t e^{-t} \right) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} l_1 e^{-t} + l_2 t e^{-t} \\ l_2 e^{-t} \end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$$

The initial condition is satisfied if

$$
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = l_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + l_2 \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} l_1 \\ l_2 \end{pmatrix},
$$

hence $l_1 = l_2 = 1$, and the unique solution of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc, @eq-2x2sys-ic with the above data is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{x}(t) &= e^{-t} \begin{pmatrix} 1 + t \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The plot of the solution is shown in @fig-example-linear-system-repeated-ev. Because $e^{-t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$, the solution converges to $(0,0)$ as $t \to \infty$. However, the solutions approach the origin in a more complex manner, not quite directly as in @fig-example-linear-system-real-evs, and not quite spiralling as in @fig-example-linear-system-complex-evs. This is the contribution of the $t$ term in the solution, and we will discuss this in more detail in @sec-phase-portraits.
:::

::: {layout="[[-25,50,-25]]"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-example-linear-system-repeated-ev
#| fig-cap: "Plot of the solution of @exm-SysLinExC."
#| echo: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from utils import apply_style, plot_phase_portrait

apply_style()

# ── System matrix ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A = [[-1,  1],
     [ 0, -1]]

# ── Start points for trajectories ────────────────────────────────────────────
starts = [( -1,  1)]

# ── Layout: info panel (top, fixed height) + phase portrait (below) ──────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 6), constrained_layout=True)
gs  = gridspec.GridSpec(2, 1, height_ratios=[1, 5], figure=fig)

ax_info = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])   # info panel — fixed height ratio
ax      = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])   # phase portrait

plot_phase_portrait(
    ax,
    A        = A,
    starts   = starts,
    xlim     = (-1.5, 1.5),
    ylim     = (-1.5, 1.5),
    t_max    = 5,
    n_grid   = 20,
    t_arrows = [1],
    alpha    = 0.4,
    backward = False,
    ax_info  = ax_info,   # pass the info panel here
)

plt.show()
```

:::

## Phase portraits {#sec-phase-portraits}

In this section we generalise the idea of a phase line that we used in @sec-differential-equations to systems of differential equations. This generalisation is called a *phase portrait* and is a very useful tool to visualise solutions to systems of differential equations, including those that we cannot solve analytically. To introduce the key ideas though, we will focus on $2\times 2$ systems of linear constant-coefficient first order autonomous differential equations.^[In @sec-autonomous-systems we will see how we can link nonlinear systems to the results discussed in this section.]

::: {.callout-important}
::: {#def-phase-portrait}
A *phase portrait* (also called *phase diagram*) of @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc is the set of curves in the $x_1$-$x_2$-plane that are parametrised by solutions to @eq-2x2sys-lin-hom-cc.
:::
:::

Note that @fig-example-linear-system-real-evs, @fig-example-linear-system-complex-evs and @fig-example-linear-system-repeated-ev are technically phase portraits, but they only show a single solution. Typically, in phase portraits, we represent a few solutions to showcase the overall behaviour of the system.

Before going into detail on how to draw phase portraits, let us talk stability. We will give a formal definition of stationary points in @sec-autonomous-systems, but for now we will just say that the definition we gave for differential equations naturally generalises. A stationary point is a point $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ that, if the solution starts there, it will stay there forever. Alternatively, we can picture it as a point for which the right-hand side of the system of differential equations is zero. For a homogeneous linear system with constant coefficients, this means

$$
A\boldsymbol{x}^* = \boldsymbol{0}, \quad \implies \quad \boldsymbol{x}^* = \boldsymbol{0},
$$ {#eq-stationary-point-linear-system}

so for the rest of the section we will focus on the stationary point at the origin.^[If @eq-stationary-point-linear-system is underdetermined, then we will have infinitely many stationary points (a line, or maybe even the whole plane). For now let us not worry about that.] We can consider the stability of this stationary point but, as we will see, a lot more complex behaviour can occur in systems of differential equations than in the one-dimensional case. We will showcase these behaviours through examples as we discuss how to draw phase portraits.

::: {.callout-important}

::: {#alg-phase-portrait}

## Drawing phase portraits

Consider a $2\times 2$ system of linear constant-coefficient first order autonomous differential equations

$$
\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}=A\boldsymbol{x}.
$$

Before any drawing, we need to compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A$ (or, if the eigenvalue is repeated, the vector $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$). Then we can follow the steps below to draw a phase portrait:

0. Draw the axes: $x_1$ and $x_2$, with the stationary point at the origin.

Now we need to consider three cases based on the eigenvalues of $A$.

**Case 1: real (distinct) eigenvalues:**

1. Draw a line through the stationary point along each eigenvalue.
2. Draw arrows on these lines:
   * Pointing towards the stationary point if the corresponding eigenvalue is negative.
   * Pointing away from the stationary point if the corresponding eigenvalue is positive.
3. Using the lines as a guide, add in additional lines demonstrating the evolution of various solutions as $t$ increases, including arrows to determine the direction of travel. As a guideline, solutions start moving parallel to the eigenvector with smallest eigenvalue (in absolute value), and then bend towards the eigenvector with largest eigenvalue (in absolute value) as $t$ increases, with the direction of travel determined by the arrows from Step 2. 

**Case 2: complex eigenvalues:**

1. Work out the direction in which solutions cross the axes. To do so, evaluate the right-hand side of the system of differential equations at a point along a given axis. The resulting vector will point in the direction of travel, i.e. the direction in which the solution spirals.^[It is actually sufficient to calculate the direction on one axis only, but it is safer to do it on both axes in practice.]
2. Draw the solutions:
   * If $p=0$ then draw circles.
   * If $p<0$ then draw inward spirals in the direction of travel.
   * If $p>0$ then draw outward spirals in the direction of travel.

In all cases, draw arrows on the spirals/circles to indicate the direction of travel.

**Case 3: repeated eigenvalue:**

1. Draw a line through the stationary point along the eigenvalue.
2. Draw arrows on the line based on the sign of the eigenvalue (like in Case 1).
3. Draw a second line through the stationary point along $\boldsymbol{v}^{(2)}$ (this time without arrows).
4. Determine the direction in which solutions cross the second line by evaluating the right-hand side of the system at points along the line. You want, at least, to evaluate one point at each side of the stationary point.
5. Using the lines as a guide, add in additional lines demonstrating the evolution of various solutions as $t$ increases, including arrows to determine the direction of travel. As a guideline, solutions start moving parallel to the eigenvector, then bend around crossing the second line in the direction determined in Step 4, and then bend back to be parallel to the eigenvector again, but in the opposite direction.

:::

::: {#rem-phase-portraits}

Phase portraits are a qualitative tool to visualise the behaviour of solutions to systems of differential equations, not a quantititative one (at least not in this module). Therefore, when you draw phase portraits, you should focus on the overall structure and behaviour of the solutions (qualitative shape, direction of travel, etc.) rather than the specific shape of the solutions or the exact points it goes through. 

:::

:::



With this information, we now draw phase portraits for various systems to showcase all the different behaviours that can occur. In each case, the details of the system (the matrix $A$, eigenvalues and eigenvectors) are shown in the plot so you can work out the results yourself.^[In the figures here we also show the grey arrows that indicate the direction of travel of the solution at each point, but you do not have to do that. Similarly, we use different colours for the different solutions for clarity, but you do not have to do that either.]

::: {.callout-important}
First we discuss the case of real eigenvalues. We need to distinguish three separate cases, based on the signs of the eigenvalues. If both eigenvalues are positive (@fig-phase-portraits-source-node), then the stationary point is unstable and is called a *source node*. If both eigenvalues are negative (@fig-phase-portraits-sink-node), then the stationary point is stable and is called a *sink node*. The source/sink node terminology comes from the fact that solutions "flow" away from the stationary point in the case of a source node, and "flow" towards the stationary point in the case of a sink node. If one eigenvalue is positive and the other is negative (@fig-phase-portraits-saddle-node), then the stationary point is unstable and is called a *saddle node*.
:::

::: {#fig-phase-portraits-real-evs layout="[[50,50],[-25,50,-25]]"}


:::

::: {.callout-important}
Next we consider the case of complex eigenvalues. If the real part of the eigenvalues is positive, then the stationary point is unstable and is called a *source spiral*. If the real part of the eigenvalues is negative, then the stationary point is stable and is called a *sink spiral*. If the real part of the eigenvalues is zero, it is called a *center*. In this case, the solution does neither converge nor diverge from the stationary point, but rather oscillates around it. As the solution does not get further and further from the stationary point as time increases, the solution is stable. Sometimes, we may refer it as marginally stable, because the solution does not converge to the stationary point either.
:::


::: {#fig-phase-portraits-complex-evs layout="[[50,50],[-25,50,-25]]"}

### Degenerate cases

::: {.callout-important}
In the classification above, we have assumed that the eigenvalues are nonzero, but they could be. In that case, the behaviour of the system is a bit different, and they are called degenerate cases. For a $2\times 2$ system, there are two degenerate cases: either one eigenvalue is zero and the other is nonzero (and real) or both eigenvalues are zero. The latter is quite simple: if both eigenvalues are zero, then the matrix $A$ is the zero matrix, therefore
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) = A \boldsymbol{x}(t) = \boldsymbol{0}, \quad \implies \quad \boldsymbol{x}(t) = \boldsymbol{x}_0,
$$
which implies that all points $\boldsymbol{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ are stationary points. As nothing happens, there is nothing we can draw in a phase portrait.

The former case is a bit more interesting. If one eigenvalue is zero and the other is nonzero, then the line through the stationary point along the eigenvector corresponding to the zero eigenvalue is a line of stationary points. To see that, consider the definition of the eigenvalue and eigenvector for $\lambda = 0$:
$$
(\lambda I - A) \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0} \quad \implies \quad A \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0},
$$
but this means that the eigenvector (and any multiple of it) satisfies the definition of a stationary point, i.e. $A \boldsymbol{x}^* = \boldsymbol{0}$. The other eigenvector (corresponding to the nonzero eigenvalue) is not a stationary point, but it is a line of solutions that either converge to or diverge from the line of stationary points, depending on the sign of the nonzero eigenvalue. In that case, the phase portrait looks as shown in @fig-phase-portraits-degenerate-case.
:::

::: {#fig-phase-portraits-degenerate-case layout="[[50,50]]"}

## Autonomous systems {#sec-autonomous-systems}

We conclude this section with a discussion of autonomous nonlinear systems. The idea is to leverage the concepts we have just introduced for phase portraits of linear systems to understand the behaviour of nonlinear systems. 

We constrain ourseles to $2 \times 2$ autonomous systems, that is systimes of the form
$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_1(t) = f_1 \left( x_1(t),x_2(t) \right), \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x_2(t) = f_2 \left( x_1(t),x_2(t) \right),
\end{split}
\quad \quad \quad t \in (\alpha,\beta)
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-auto}

with some given functions $f_1,f_2: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$. Remember that, as the system is autonomous, these functions $f_i$ do not depend on the independent variable $t$.

We can also use the vector notation and write @eq-2x2sys-auto as
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \boldsymbol{x}(t) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}(t)), \quad \quad \quad t \in (\alpha,\beta),
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-auto-matrix}
where $\boldsymbol{x}(t) = (x_1(t),x_2(t))^T$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}) = (f_1(\boldsymbol{x}),f_2(\boldsymbol{x}))^T$. This is analogous to the vector notation we used for linear systems in @eq-2x2sys-lin-matrix.

Let us now give a more formal definition of a stationary point and its stability.

::: {.callout-important}

::: {#def-stationary-point-systemw}

## Stationary point

A *stationary point* of @eq-2x2sys-auto-matrix is a point $\boldsymbol{x}^* \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}^*) = \boldsymbol{0}$, i.e. $f_1(\boldsymbol{x}^*) = 0$ and $f_2(\boldsymbol{x}^*) = 0$.

:::

::: {#def-stable-stationary-point-system}

## Stability

The stationary solution (or point) of @eq-2x2sys-auto-matrix is called *stable* if solutions $(x_1(t),x_2(t))$ that start nearby remain close as time $t$ increases.^[A precise definition of stability will be given in follow-up modules once measuring distances and limits will have been discussed in greater depth.] It is called *unstable* if solutions that start nearby do not remain close as time $t$ increases.
:::
:::

::: {#exm-lotka-volterra}

## Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model

Let us consider a model that describes the interaction between two species in a predator-prey relationship, which is known as the Lotka-Volterra model. Let $x(t)$ be the population of prey and $y(t)$ the population of predators at time $t$. The model is given by the following system of differential equations:

$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} x(t) &= \alpha x(t) - \beta x(t) y(t), \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} y(t) &= -\gamma y(t) + \delta x(t) y(t),
\end{split}
\quad \quad \quad t \in \mathbb{R},
$$ {#eq-lotka-volterra}

with given parameters $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta>0$. The first equation describes the growth of the prey population, which grows at a rate $\alpha$ in the absence of predators, but is reduced by the presence of predators at a rate $\beta$. The second equation describes the growth of the predator population, which decreases at a rate $\gamma$ in the absence of prey, but increases at a rate $\delta$ due to the presence of prey. Note that the interaction term between the two species is proportional to the product of their populations, which reflects the idea that more prey leads to more food for predators, and more predators leads to more predation on prey.

Let us now determine the stationary points of this system $x^*$ and $y^*$. They have to satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha x^* - \beta x^* y^* &= 0, \\
-\gamma y^* + \delta x^* y^* &= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations simultaneously, we find that the stationary points are $(x^*,y^*) = (0,0)$ and $(x^*,y^*) = (\gamma/\delta,\alpha/\beta)$. The first stationary point corresponds to the extinction of both species, while the second stationary point corresponds to a stable coexistence of both species.

:::

We have now seen how to calculate stationary points of a nonlinear system, but how do we determine their stability? In order to do so, we can linearise the system around the stationary point and study the resulting linear system using the tools in @sec-phase-portraits.

Let $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$ denote a stationary solution (or point) of @eq-2x2sys-auto. In order to get some more insight into whether $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$ is stable we study solutions of the form

$$
(x_1(t),x_2(t)) = (x^*_1 + \xi_1(t), x^*_2 + \xi_2(t))
$$

where $(\xi_1(t),\xi_2(t))$ is a "small" deviation from the stationary point.^[In order to properly formulate what "small" means, one needs to nondimensionalise the problem.] If we take the time derivative of both sides, we get 

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} (x_1(t),x_2(t)) = \tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} (\xi_1(t),\xi_2(t)),$$ 

so that the system for $(\xi_1(t),\xi_2(t))$ becomes

$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \xi_1(t) = f_1 \left( x^*_1 + \xi_1(t), x^*_2 + \xi_2(t) \right), \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \xi_2(t) = f_2 \left( x^*_1 + \xi_1(t), x^*_2 + \xi_2(t) \right),
\end{split}
\quad \quad \quad t \in (\alpha,\beta).
$$

Now, we take a Taylor expansion^[You are probably familiar with Taylor expansions for functions of a single variable: $f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$. For functions of multiple variables, the idea is similar, but one needs to take partial derivatives with respect to each variable while keeping the others fixed.] of the right-hand-side around the stationary point $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$. Let us work first with the first equation. We have that

$$
f_1 \left( x^*_1 + \xi_1(t), x^*_2 + \xi_2(t) \right) \approx f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_1(t) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_2(t),
$$
where we have dropped the higher order terms, hence the $\approx$. Here, the *partial derivatives* $\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_1}$ and $\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}$ with respect to the first and second argument of the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ appear. There are defined by differentiating with respect to one argument whilst keeping the other fixed, for instance,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_1 (x_1,x_2) = \lim_{\Delta x_2 \to 0} \frac{f_1(x_1,x_2 + \Delta x_2) - f_1(x_1,x_2)}{\Delta x_2}.
$$

Then, because $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$ is a stationary point, we have that $f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) = 0$, so that the first term on the right-hand-side vanishes. A similar expansion can be done for the second equation, and we obtain

$$
\begin{split}
f_1 \left( x^*_1 + \xi_1(t), x^*_2 + \xi_2(t) \right) \approx \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_1(t) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_2(t), \\
f_2 \left( x^*_1 + \xi_1(t), x^*_2 + \xi_2(t) \right) \approx \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_2(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_1(t) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_2(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_2(t).
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-fexpand}

::: {.callout-important}
With this approximation we obtain the following system for $(\xi_1(t),\xi_2(t))$:

$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \xi_1(t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_1(t) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_2(t), \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \xi_2(t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_2(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_1(t) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_2(x^*_1,x^*_2) \xi_2(t),
\end{split}
\quad \quad \quad t \in (\alpha,\beta).
$$ {#eq-2x2sys-linearised}

This system is *linear* in $(\xi_1(t),\xi_2(t))$. We therefore talk about a *linearisation* of @eq-2x2sys-auto around the stationary solution $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$. In particular, the coefficients $\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2)$, etc. are constant, and in that case we can find explicit solutions.

The *principle of linearised stability* now relates the stability properties of the original system @eq-2x2sys-auto around the stationary point $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$ to the stability properties of the linearised system @eq-2x2sys-linearised around $(0,0)$. Roughly, the stationary point is stable if and only if the linearised system is stable around the origin.

:::


::: {#rem-jacobian}

As we have seen, it is often more convenient to write linear systems in matrix form. In that case, the linearised system @eq-2x2sys-linearised can be written as
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{\mathrm{d}}t} \begin{pmatrix} \xi_1(t) \\ \xi_2(t) \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) & \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_1(x^*_1,x^*_2) \\[0.3em] \frac{\partial}{\partial x_1} f_2(x^*_1,x^*_2) & \frac{\partial}{\partial x_2} f_2(x^*_1,x^*_2) \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \xi_1(t) \\ \xi_2(t) \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The matrix on the right-hand-side is called the *Jacobian* of the system @eq-2x2sys-auto at the stationary point $(x^*_1,x^*_2)$, and is denoted by $J(x^*_1,x^*_2)$. The Jacobian is a $2 \times 2$ matrix that contains all the partial derivatives of the functions $f_1$ and $f_2$ evaluated at the stationary point.^[You will learn more about Jacobians in the follow-up module [MA145 Mathematical Methods and Modelling 2](https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/currentstudents/modules/ma145/).]

:::

::: {#exm-linearised-lotka-volterra}

## Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model (continued)

Let us linearise the predator-prey model @eq-lotka-volterra around the stationary points. We will compute the Jacobian matrix first, and then evaluate it at the stationary points. The Jacobian matrix is given by

$$
J(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \alpha - \beta y & -\beta x \\\delta y & -\gamma + \delta x \end{pmatrix}.
$$

First we study the stationary point $(x^*,y^*) = (0,0)$. Evaluating the Jacobian at this point gives
$$
J(0,0) = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & 0 \\ 0 & -\gamma \end{pmatrix}.
$$

This is already a diagonal matrix, and we can read off the eigenvalues as $\lambda_1 = \alpha > 0$ and $\lambda_2 = -\gamma < 0$. Therefore, the stationary point $(0,0)$ is a saddle point, and hence unstable. A side note, if there is only predators present in the system, then they will die out, as there is no food for them. This is consistent with the definition of a saddle point, because having only predators corresponds to starting on the $y$-axis, which is the direction of the eigenvector corresponding to the negative eigenvalue.

Next we study the stationary point $(x^*,y^*) = (\gamma/\delta,\alpha/\beta)$. Evaluating the Jacobian at this point gives
$$
J\left(\frac{\gamma}{\delta}, \frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\beta \frac{\gamma}{\delta} \\ \delta \frac{\alpha}{\beta} & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Now the eigenvalues of the matrix satisfy $\lambda^2 + \alpha \gamma = 0$, which gives 

$$\lambda_{1,2} = \pm i \sqrt{\alpha \gamma}.$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, and the stationary point $(\gamma/\delta,\alpha/\beta)$ is a centre. This means that the populations of both species will oscillate around this stationary point, and the system is stable in the sense that the populations will not diverge to infinity.

Let us now visualise the phase portrait of the Lotka-Volterra system around the non-zero stationary point, @fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra. We take the parameters $\alpha = 3$, $\beta = 2$, $\gamma = 2$, and $\delta = 1$ and compare the true solution (obtained numerically) with the linearise solution for a starting point $(x, y) = (1.5, 1)$ (@fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra-far). We observe that, even though the quantitative agreement is not perfect, the qualitative behaviour is captured well by the linearised system. In particular, the linearised system captures the oscillatory behaviour of the populations around the stationary point. Note that if instead we start much closer to the stationary point (@fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra-closer), then the agreement between the true solution and the linearised solution is much better, as expected.^[Note that @fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra-closer has a narrower plotting range than @fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra-far, which magnifies the discrepancy between solutions.]

::: {#fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra layout="[[50,50]]"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra-far
#| fig-cap: "Starting point $(x, y) = (1.5, 1)$."
#| echo: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from utils import apply_style, plot_phase_portrait_nonlinear

apply_style()

alpha = 3
beta = 2
gamma = 2
delta = 1

def lotka_volterra(t, y):
    x_1, x_2 = y
    dx1dt = alpha * x_1 - beta * x_1 * x_2
    dx2dt = delta * x_1 * x_2 - gamma * x_2
    return [dx1dt, dx2dt]

def linearised(t, y):
    x_1, x_2 = y
    dx1dt =  - beta * gamma / delta * (x_2 - alpha / beta)
    dx2dt = delta * alpha / beta * (x_1 - gamma / delta)
    return [dx1dt, dx2dt]

starts1 = [(1.5, 1)]
starts2 = starts1

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5), constrained_layout=True)

# System 1 — with vector field
plot_phase_portrait_nonlinear(
    ax,
    rhs         = lotka_volterra,
    starts      = starts1,
    xlim        = (0, 4),
    ylim        = (0, 4),
    traj_color  = "steelblue",
    axis_labels = ("$x$", "$y$"),
    show_ticks  = True,
    show_field  = True,
)

# System 2 — overlay, no vector field
plot_phase_portrait_nonlinear(
    ax,
    rhs         = linearised,
    starts      = starts2,
    xlim        = (0, 4),
    ylim        = (0, 4),
    traj_color  = "tomato",
    axis_labels = ("$x$", "$y$"),
    show_ticks  = True,
    show_field  = False,
)

plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-phase-portrait-lotka-volterra-closer
#| fig-cap: "Starting point $(x, y) = (2.1, 1.4)$."
```

Phase portraits for the Lotka-Volterra system, taking $\alpha = 3$, $\beta = 2$, $\gamma = 2$, and $\delta = 1$, for two different initial conditions. The exact solution is shown in blue, while the linearised system is shown in red.
